title: Aristotle’s Four Causes
subtitle: Four kinds of ‘because’
learning_objective: See that ‘why does this exist?’ has four different kinds of answer in Aristotle — material, formal, efficient and final cause — and that they are kinds of explanation, not modern forces or variables.
disclaimer: A teaching version of Aristotle’s four causes. It shows how he sorted explanations; it does not claim that every thing has a purpose.

steps.title: Judge
steps.prompt: Why does it exist? Choose the one best answer.
options: Because of what it’s made of
Because someone or something made it

steps.title: Experiment
steps.prompt: Tap a card, then tap the kind of cause it answers. Two cards don’t belong at all.

steps.title: Judge again
steps.prompt: How many ‘becauses’ does a full explanation need, for Aristotle?
options: Four kinds, each answering a different question

steps.title: Explain
steps.prompt: What the four causes are — and are not.

steps.title: Apply
steps.prompt: Explain something of your own with all four.

steps.title: Keep
steps.prompt: Keep what you understood and what you still wonder about.

user_actions.label: Place a card on a cause

feedback_rules.say: Good. Now try to give the single reason it exists.
You picked one kind of answer. Aristotle would say the others are also answers — to different questions.
Yes — that card answers that kind of ‘why’.
That card answers a different kind of ‘why’. Ask: made of? form? made by? for what?
That one isn’t any of the four causes — it comes from modern science.
All four in place. Each answers a different question about the same thing.
That is Aristotle’s view: a full explanation can involve all four kinds of cause.
Today we often look for one cause — but Aristotle counts four kinds, each answering its own question.
Partly right: for natural things, form and purpose often coincide — but the four questions can always be asked.

slots.label: Formal cause
slots.q: What form makes it what it is?

layers.title: ① Four kinds of explanation
layers.body: For Aristotle, knowing a thing means knowing its ‘why’, and there are four kinds: what it is made of (material), the form or structure that makes it what it is (formal), what brought it about (efficient), and what it is for (final).
layers.source: Aristotle, Physics II.3; Metaphysics V.2 (Δ.2) — check against your edition

layers.title: ② Purpose in nature
layers.body: Aristotle applied final causes to natural things too: an acorn grows towards being an oak. For living things, form and purpose often coincide. Whether nature really has purposes (teleology) is one of the most debated parts of his view.

layers.title: ③ Not modern forces
layers.body: The four causes are kinds of explanation, not physical forces and not experimental variables. Modern science mostly keeps the efficient cause (and the material), and talks about function in its own terms. That is why ‘gravity’ and ‘a variable’ had no slot.
layers.source: See e.g. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Aristotle on Causality”
layers.maps_to: The two cards with no slot
